edits.english: The Gemara recounts an incident involving a certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer. Rav deemed that barrel of beer forbidden. The Sages said before Rav Sheshet: Shall we say that Rav maintains that even in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden? For the mouse's taste certainly detracts!

It is related: A certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer. Rav deemed that beer forbidden. The Sages said before Rav Sheshet: Shall we say that Rav maintains that even in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden? For the mouse's taste certainly detracts!

edits.hebrew: ההוא עכברא דנפל בגו חביתא דשיכרא אסריה רב לההוא שיכרא - תימה: דהא צונן בצונן הוא ולשתרי? וי"ל דמיירי ששהה שם יום או יומיים, והיה כבוש בתוך השכר, וכבוש הרי הוא כמבושל:

edits.english: A certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer, Rav deemed that beer forbidden - It is astonishing: For it is a cold item in a cold item, and it should be permitted! One can say that it refers to a case where it remained there for a day or two, and was pickled in the beer, and a pickled item is considered as if it was cooked.

edits.hebrew: והכא - גבי שרץ, היינו טעמא דאסור בפגם:

edits.english: But here - With regard to a creeping animal, that is the reason it is forbidden even if it imparts a detrimental flavor:

edits.hebrew: דהא - איסור שרץ חידוש הוא:

edits.english: As it is - The prohibition of a creeping animal is a novelty:

edits.hebrew: דהא מימאיס - ובלאו אזהרה, בדילין אינשי מיניה. ולמה ליה דאזהר רחמנא עליה? שמע מינה: אפילו נותן טעם לפגם אסור:

edits.english: As it is repulsive - And without a warning, people distance themselves from it. So why did the Merciful One warn about it? Learn from this: Even if it imparts a detrimental flavor, it is forbidden:

Rav Sheshet said to them: Rav generally maintains that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But here, in the case of a mouse and similar creatures, it is a unique novelty that the Torah introduced, as it is repulsive and people distance themselves from it on their own. And even so, the Merciful One prohibited it. Therefore, even if it imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is still forbidden, unlike what we learned from an animal carcass.

edits.hebrew: אלא מעתה - אי חידוש הוא:

edits.english: If that is so - If it is a novelty:

edits.hebrew: יטמא לח ויבש - שהרי מאוס הוא, ובדילי אינשי ממגעו. למה ליה דאזהר רחמנא עליה? שמע מינה: אפילו כשהוא יבש מטמא:

edits.english: It should impart ritual impurity whether moist or dried out - For it is repulsive, and people distance themselves from touching it. Why did the Merciful One warn about it? Learn from this: Even when it is dry, it imparts impurity:

edits.hebrew: אלמה תנן - במסכת נדה (דף נד:): "אבל השרץ ושכבת זרע מטמאין לחין ואין מטמאין יבשין". אלא לאו שמע מינה: לא מאיס שרץ ולאו חידוש, ואיצטריך לאזהורי עליה דעובדי כוכבים אכלי:

edits.english: Why did we learn - In Tractate Niddah (page 54b): "But a creeping animal and semen impart impurity when moist but do not impart impurity when dry." Rather, must we not conclude from this: A creeping animal is not repulsive, and it is not a novelty, and it was necessary to warn about it because gentiles eat it:

The Sages said to Rav Sheshet: If that is so, according to your explanation that it is a novelty and comes to be more stringent than other prohibitions, then the mouse and similar creatures should impart ritual impurity whether they are moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna: Carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity when they are moist but do not impart impurity when they are dried out?

edits.hebrew: וליטעמיך שכבת זרע - הא ודאי ממאיס, ובדילי אינשי ממגעו, וחידוש הוא, תטמא לח ויבש:

edits.english: And according to your reasoning, semen - This is certainly repulsive, and people distance themselves from touching it, and it is a novelty, so it should impart impurity whether moist or dried out:

Rav Sheshet said to them: And according to your reasoning, by which you compare the law of ritual impurity to the law of forbidden foods, semen, which is also repulsive, should impart impurity whether moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna: With regard to semen and creeping animals, they impart impurity when they are moist but do not impart impurity when they are dried out?

Rather, what have you to say? With regard to the ritual impurity of semen, the Merciful One states in the verse: “The flow of seed” (Leviticus 15:16), meaning that the reference is to semen that is fit to fertilize. Here too, with regard to the ritual impurity of a mouse, the verse states: “When they have died” (Leviticus 11:32). The Merciful One states that the carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity only when they are similar to the creeping animals' state at time of their death, i.e., when they are still moist. Therefore, there is no contradiction to the claim that the prohibition against eating a mouse is a novelty and consequently applies even when it detracted from the flavor of the food into which it fell.

edits.hebrew: אלא - שאני לענין טומאה, אע"ג דחידוש הוא, גזירת הכתוב היא דלח ולא יבש, דכתיב: "כל אשר יפול עליו מהם במותם", כעין מותם, כשהן לחין:

edits.english: Rather - It is different concerning ritual impurity. Even though it is a novelty, it is a decree of the verse that it is impure when moist but not when dry, as it is written: "whatever any of them falls upon, when they are dead" (Leviticus 11:32), meaning similar to their death, when they are moist:

edits.hebrew: שכבת זרע אמר רחמנא בראויה להזריע - "או איש אשר תצא ממנו שכבת זרע":

edits.english: The Merciful One states "semen" concerning that which is fit to fertilize - "When a man has an emission of semen" (Leviticus 15:16):

Rather, what do you have to say? The Merciful One states: "Semen" (Leviticus 15:16). That is to say, it is a Torah decree that it imparts impurity only when it is moist, when it is fit to fertilize. Here too, regarding a mouse and similar creatures, the Merciful One states: "When they have died" (Leviticus 11:32) – meaning that they impart impurity only similar to their death, as they were at the time of their death. Therefore, when they are dry, they no longer impart impurity. And from this, there is no contradiction to the statement that the prohibition against eating a mouse is a novelty and it is forbidden even when it imparts a detrimental flavor.

edits.hebrew: דמתא - עכבר של יישוב מאיס:

edits.english: A city mouse - A mouse from a settlement is repulsive:

edits.hebrew: עכבר דדברא - אשקור"ל בלע"ז:

edits.english: A field mouse - écureuil in Old French:

edits.ref: Otzar La'azei Rashi, Talmud, Avodah Zarah 142
edits.english:
1906 / (Avodah Zarah 69a.) / Mouse
אישקורי"ל / squirrel / Squirrel
Here, in contrast to Sanhedrin 91a. (above, no. 1722), it is not a common mouse, but a field mouse. But even a field mouse is different from our squirrel.
✭ squirrel

Rav Shimi of Neharde’a objects to this assumption that we raised: And is the mouse repulsive? But isn’t it served at the table of kings, considered by them a choice food! Rav Shimi of Neharde’a said: This is not difficult. This statement, that a mouse is served as a delicacy, is stated with regard to a field mouse, which is served at the table of kings, and that statement, that it is repulsive, is stated with regard to a city mouse, which is repulsive to everyone.

Rava said: The halakha is that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But with regard to a mouse that fell into beer, I do not know what Rav's reason was for prohibiting it. Is it because he maintains that generally, if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden, and the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion? Or is it because he maintains that generally, if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted, but a mouse that falls into beer enhances its flavor, and therefore it is forbidden?

edits.hebrew: אמר רבא: הלכתא נותן טעם לפגם כו' - פירוש: אף בשרצים. ולא תימא דבשרצים חידוש כדקאמר לעיל, וליתסר משום פגם דשרצים, אלא אף בשרצים פגם מותר. ועכברא בשיכרא דאסר, לא ידענא אי משום נותן טעם לפגם דקסבר אסור [אף בשאר שרצים], ולית הלכתא כוותיה; פירוש: דאף בשאר שרצים פגם מותר. אי משום דאשבוחי קמשבח. וא"ת: וליפשוט ליה טעמיה דרב מההיא דפרק קמא דחולין (דף ח: ושם ד"ה השוחט): "השוחט בסכין של עובדי כוכבים, רב אמר קולף ושמואל אמר מדיח", ואע"ג דסתם כלי עובדי כוכבים אינם בני יומן, דהשתא הוי לפגם. וי"ל דהתם מיירי בידוע שנשתמשו בו ביום. א"נ, התם טעמא משום שמנונית דאיסור הנדבק בדופני הסכין, שהוא בעין והוי לשבח גם כשאינו בן יומו. וא"ת: מאי קאמר הכא "לא ידענא אי אשבוחי משבח"? ליטעמיה קפילא ארמאה! וי"ל דשמא עכברא בשיכרא מחזק את השכר ומחמצו, והשתא כשנתחזק השכר, אין ידוע אם מחמת השכר עצמו. וקי"ל כרבא דאמר נותן טעם לפגם מותר אף בשרצים, ונפקא מינה דכשאינו בת יומו וכיוצא בו מותר אף בשרצים:

edits.english: Rava said: The halakha is that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to its detriment, etc. - This means even with creeping animals. And do not say that with creeping animals it is a novelty, as stated above, and it should be forbidden due to the detrimental flavor of creeping animals. Rather, even with creeping animals, a detrimental flavor is permitted. And regarding the mouse in beer that Rav prohibited, I do not know if it is because he holds that imparting a detrimental flavor is forbidden [even with other creeping animals], and the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion; meaning, that even with other creeping animals, a detrimental flavor is permitted. Or if it is because it enhances the flavor. And if you ask: Why doesn't he resolve Rav's reasoning from that which is stated in the first chapter of Hullin (page 8b, and there, s.v. HaShochet): "One who slaughters with a gentile's knife, Rav says one must peel, and Shmuel says one must rinse," even though gentile's vessels are usually not bat yoma, so it would be detrimental. One can say that there it deals with a case where it is known that it was used on that day. Alternatively, there the reason is due to the fatty residue of the forbidden substance clinging to the sides of the knife, which is tangible and enhances the flavor even when it is not bat yoma. And if you ask: What does he mean here by "I do not know if it enhances the flavor"? Let an Aramaic taster taste it! One can say that perhaps the mouse in beer strengthens the beer and makes it sour, and now that the beer is strengthened, it is not known if it is due to the beer itself. And we rule in accordance with Rava, who says that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted even with creeping animals, and the practical implication is that when it is not bat yoma and similar cases, it is permitted even with creeping animals:
A dilemma was raised before them (the students):

If a mouse fell into vinegar, what is the halakha? Does the mouse enhance its flavor? Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi: There was such an incident in the study hall of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden. This indicates that it enhances the flavor. Rav Ashi said to him: This is not a proof. That mouse was dismembered, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden due to concern that one might consume a substantive piece of the mouse in the vinegar, which is prohibited regardless of the taste.

edits.hebrew: נפל לגו חלא מאי - מי אמרינן: החומץ טעמו קשה, ואין השרץ מפיגו לתת בו טעם?

edits.english: If it fell into vinegar, what is the halakha? Do we say: The vinegar has a strong taste, and the creeping animal does not detract from it to impart a flavor?

edits.hebrew: אימרטוטי אימרטט - לחתיכות דקות קטנות, ושרץ איסורו בכעדשה כטומאתו, וחיישינן דלמא בולע חתיכות שרץ בהדי חומץ:

edits.english: It was dismembered - Into small, thin pieces. And the prohibition of a creeping animal is with a lentil-sized amount, like its impurity, and we are concerned that one might swallow pieces of the creeping animal along with the vinegar:

It is related: If a mouse fell into vinegar, what is its law? Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi: There was such an incident in the house of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana prohibited that vinegar. From this, it is inferred that it imparts an enhancing flavor and disqualifies the mixture. Rav Ashi said to him: There is no proof from there. That mouse was dismembered into small pieces, and Rav Kahana prohibited it due to the concern that one might come to eat an actual piece of the mouse within the vinegar.

edits.hebrew: איבעיא להו: נפל לגו חלא כו' - וא"ת: מ"ש משאר איסורין כמו בשיכרא? וי"ל: משום דחלא חזק מאד, ואגב חורפיה נותן טעם לשבח כמו גבי חילתית. או דלמא מעט השרץ נגד המשקה, וא"כ אין לנו לאסור כל כך. ולכך היה שואל: מה יהיה ממנו?

edits.english: A dilemma was raised before them: If it fell into vinegar, etc. - And if you ask: What is the difference from other forbidden substances, like in beer? One can say: Because vinegar is very strong, and due to its sharpness, it imparts an enhancing flavor, like with asafoetida. Or perhaps the creeping animal is small compared to the liquid, and if so, we should not prohibit it so much. And that is why he asked: What will be its fate?

edits.hebrew: ההוא אימרטוטי אימרטט - יש לתמוה: עכשיו היאך אנו אוכלים דבש דבורים, והלא רגלי הדבורים מעורבים בדבש? ואף על גב דהוי פגם, מ"מ השרץ עצמו דאיפגם מיתסר לכ"ע. לכ"נ לר"ת דודאי רגלי הדבורים כיון דעצמות בעלמא נינהו, מותרים. דהא העצמות טהורים, דתנן במסכת (טהרות פרק א): "עצמות החמור טהורות", ורגלי הדבורים כעצמות החמור. והא דאמרינן: "אברים אין להם שיעור אפילו פחות מכזית מן המת ופחות מכעדשה מן השרץ", היינו לענין טומאה, וכגון דאיכא בשר עלויה. הא לאו הכי, טהורין. ולענין אכילה, שפיר דמי:

edits.english: That one was dismembered - It is astonishing: How do we eat bee honey now? Are not bee legs mixed in the honey? And even though it is a detrimental flavor, nevertheless the creeping animal itself, which is detrimental, is forbidden to everyone. Therefore, it seems to Rabbeinu Tam that certainly bee legs, since they are mere bones, are permitted. For bones are pure, as we learned in Tractate Tahorot (Chapter 1): "The bones of a donkey are pure," and bee legs are like donkey bones. And that which we say: "Limbs have no minimum measure, even less than an olive-sized amount from a corpse and less than a lentil-sized amount from a creeping animal," this is concerning impurity, and when there is flesh on them. But if not so, they are pure. And concerning eating, it is certainly permitted:

It is related: Ravina thought to calculate the amount of vinegar necessary to nullify the mouse at 101 times its volume. He said: It should not be worse, meaning, it is not more stringent, than teruma, as we learned in a mishna: Teruma is nullified in a mixture by 101 times its volume. Rav Taḥlifa bar Giza said to Ravina: Perhaps this case is similar to spice of teruma in a pot, whose flavor is not nullified by 101 times its volume, but by more than that!

edits.hebrew: סבר לשעורי בק"א, אמר: לא גרע מתרומה כו' - תימה: נהי דתרומה נינהו, כשהוא בקדרה בדבר לח בטלה בס'. כדאמר פרק גיד הנשה (חולין דף צז.): "קדירה שבשל בה תרומה, לא יבשל בה חולין, ואם בשל בנותן טעם". וי"ל דס"ל: כיון שטעמו חזק בשכר, יש לדמותו לתרומה לדבר יבש. וא"ת: אמאי לא בטיל באחד ומאתים כמו ערלה וכלאי הכרם? וי"ל דשאני התם משום דהוו איסור הנאה, לכך לא ילפינן מיניה שרצים דשרו בהנאה, אבל תרומה שרי בהנאה:

edits.english: He thought to calculate it at 101, he said: It is not worse than teruma, etc. - It is astonishing: Granted that it is teruma, when it is in a pot with a liquid, it is nullified by 60, as stated in the chapter Gid HaNashe (Hullin page 97a): "A pot in which teruma was cooked, one should not cook non-sacred food in it, and if one cooked, it is forbidden if it imparts flavor." One can say that he holds: Since its taste is strong in beer, it should be compared to teruma in a dry item. And if you ask: Why is it not nullified by 200, like orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard? One can say that there it is different because they are prohibitions of benefit, therefore we do not derive from them creeping animals, which are permitted for benefit. But teruma is permitted for benefit:

edits.hebrew: כתבלין ופלפלין דלא בטיל טעמייהו - לא בס' ולא בק', שהרי מעט תבלין נותן טעם בקדרה גדולה. אבל אין לומר דלא בטיל כלל, דהא בהדי נותן טעם חשבינן ליה ולא בהדי אוסרין במשהו. כדקאמר לעיל (עבודה זרה דף סו.): "תבלין של שלשה שמות אסור ומצטרף" כו':

edits.english: Like spices and peppers whose flavor is not nullified - Not by 60 nor by 100, for a small amount of spice imparts flavor in a large pot. But one cannot say that it is not nullified at all, for we consider it among those that impart flavor, and not among those that prohibit with any amount. As stated above (Avodah Zarah page 66a): "Spices of three names are forbidden and combine," etc.:

edits.hebrew: בחמשין - כיון דחומץ טעמו קשה, לא בעי שתין לבטוליה, דאפילו בחמשין לא יהיב ביה טעמא:

edits.english: At fifty - Since vinegar has a strong taste, it does not require sixty to nullify it, for even at fifty, it does not impart its flavor:

It is further related: Rav Aḥai calculated the amount of vinegar necessary to nullify the mouse at fifty times its volume. He held that sharp-tasting vinegar does not require sixty times the volume, like other prohibitions in the Torah, to nullify the mouse's flavor. And Rav Shmuel, son of Rav Ika, calculated the amount of beer necessary for nullifying the mouse at sixty times the volume of the mouse.

edits.hebrew: שיער בחלא בחמשין - תימה: מ"ש דלעיל רוצה להחמיר בו אפילו יותר מס' וק', וכאן מיקל בו? וי"ל: משום דקסבר דבחלא לא אשבח כ"כ כמו בשיכרא:

edits.english: He calculated it at fifty in vinegar - It is astonishing: What is the difference that above he wants to be stringent with it even more than 60 and 100, and here he is lenient with it? One can say: Because he holds that in vinegar, it does not enhance the flavor as much as in beer:

edits.hebrew: ה"ג וכן כל איסור שבתורה - בששים. וכן הלכה רווחת בישראל: דמין בשאינו מינו בששים, חוץ מחמץ. אבל מין במינו מוקמינן בפסחים (דף ל.): הלכתא במשהו כרב, וטעמא משום דכל איסורין שבתורה מין במינו במשהו כרב, ובחמץ גזירה שאינו מינו אטו מינו:

edits.english: This is how it is taught: And so is the ruling for all prohibitions in the Torah - With sixty. And so is the widespread halakha in Israel: that a substance of one kind in a mixture not of its kind is nullified by sixty, except for ḥametz. But a substance of its own kind, we establish in Pesahim (page 30a): The halakha is that it is nullified by any amount, like Rav. And the reason is that all prohibitions in the Torah, a substance of its own kind is nullified by any amount, like Rav. And with ḥametz, it is a decree that a substance not of its kind is like a substance of its own kind:

On the Presence of a Rat in Wine or Beer
In a mixture, the dormouse gives a pleasant flavor: previously, moreover, important people regarded it as a delicacy. It is not known if the rat, which lives in dwellings, alters or improves the flavor of wine and vinegar. When a rat falls into vinegar or cold beer, this liquid is permitted if, within twenty-four hours, the rat is removed whole. But if the same liquid is hot or cold and the rat is removed whole or in pieces after a stay of twenty-four hours, the liquid is permitted if it can be filtered, contains no trace of the rat, and is sixty times greater in volume than the animal.
GLOSS: Only the presence of an insect is to be feared, not that of other forbidden things.

On the Mixing of Forbidden Food with Permitted Food and Dissolution
When a forbidden food is mixed with a permitted food of a different nature, for example, when forbidden fat is mixed with meat, the mixture must be tasted by a gentile. If the gentile says that they do not detect the flavor of the forbidden food, or if they do detect it but find it altered, the mixture is permitted, provided that the forbidden food has not subsequently improved the taste of the mixture; but the gentile must not be made aware that their opinion is needed. If there is no gentile to taste the mixture, the permitted food must be sixty times the amount of the forbidden food. The same applies to a mixture of two foods, one forbidden and one permitted, but both of the same nature, making tasting ineffective; in this case, the permitted food must be sixty times the forbidden food.
GLOSS: Nowadays it is customary not to have the mixture tasted by a gentile; it suffices to evaluate if the quantity of the permitted food is sixty times that of the forbidden food.

Milk Falling into a Meat Pot
When a piece of meat the size of an olive falls into a container of hot milk, the milk is tasted by a gentile; if he detects the taste of meat, the milk is forbidden; otherwise, it is permitted, even if it does not present a quantity sixty times greater than the meat. But the piece of meat is forbidden. However, this is only if the piece of meat was extracted before it had released the absorbed milk, i.e., it was extracted before the boiling ceased; but if it was extracted later, even if the gentile detects no meat taste when tasting it, it is forbidden unless it presents a quantity sixty times greater than the meat.
GLOSS: See further, § 98, where it is said that we do not rely on a gentile's tasting, and therefore, we always require a quantity sixty times greater.
And they conclude: And the halakha is: This and that, both are nullified by sixty times its volume, and so is the ruling for all prohibitions in the Torah, generally nullified by sixty.

edits.hebrew: אידי ואידי - פירוש: בשיכרא וחלא בשיתין. בהלכות גדולות ובירושלמי קאמר דשרץ לא בטיל כי אם באלף, ותלמודינו עיקר דבטל בששים כשאר איסורים:

edits.english: This and that - Meaning, in beer and vinegar, by sixty. In Halakhot Gedolot and in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says that a creeping animal is not nullified except by a thousand, but our Talmud is primary, that it is nullified by sixty, like other prohibitions:
